content: Shigellosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria of the genus Shigella. These bacteria are gram-negative, non-motile, facultatively anaerobic, and do not form spores. The disease was first identified in 1896 by Dr. Kiyoshi Shiga during an outbreak of bacillary dysentery in Japan. Transmission typically occurs via the fecal-oral route, particularly in areas with poor sanitation. While anyone can contract shigellosis, young children, elderly individuals, and immunocompromised patients are at higher risk. The clinical symptoms of shigellosis usually begin 12 hours to 3 days after ingesting the bacteria. Patients often experience diffuse, cramping abdominal pain, fever, and diarrhea that may contain mucus or blood. These symptoms generally resolve on their own within 5 to 7 days. However, in some cases, complications such as post-infectious arthritis (Reiter's syndrome) or hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) can occur. Diagnosis involves blood and stool tests to confirm the infection and guide antibiotic selection. Treatment primarily focuses on replacing lost fluids and electrolytes, as dehydration is a common concern. Antibiotic therapy is also recommended for all patients, typically using a 3-day course of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin, or azithromycin, depending on the strain's resistance profile. Antimotility agents should be avoided, as they can prolong the infection. There is currently no vaccine for shigellosis, so prevention relies on proper hand hygiene and safe food and water practices. The pathophysiology of shigellosis involves the bacteria invading the epithelial cells of the large intestine. Shigella uses specialized cells called M cells to enter the intestinal lining, where it invades macrophages and induces their apoptosis. This triggers inflammation, the release of proinflammatory cytokines, and the recruitment of neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes). The resulting inflammation and loss of intestinal barrier integrity lead to impaired fluid and nutrient absorption, causing diarrhea. Gross pathology often reveals hyperemia, ulcers, and edema, while microscopic findings include neutrophil infiltration and inflammatory pseudomembranes. Shigella species are classified into four serogroups: Shigella dysenteriae, Shigella flexneri, Shigella boydii, and Shigella sonnei. In developed countries, Shigella sonnei is the most common cause of shigellosis, while Shigella flexneri predominates in developing regions. Globally, there are over 160 million cases of shigellosis annually, with more than 95% occurring in developing countries. Children aged 2 to 5 years are the most commonly affected demographic, although there is no gender or racial predisposition. Risk factors for shigellosis include young age (particularly children aged 2 to 5), advanced age, immunosuppression (e.g., HIV-positive individuals), travel to areas with poor sanitation, and certain sexual practices, such as anal intercourse. The disease is self-limiting in most cases, but high-risk populations are more likely to develop complications. Prognosis is generally excellent for immunocompetent individuals, but factors such as prolonged illness, complications, or infection in high-risk patients can worsen outcomes. The diagnosis of shigellosis begins with a thorough history and physical examination. Symptoms range from mild abdominal discomfort to severe colicky pain, often accompanied by watery diarrhea that progresses to dysentery. Fever, nausea, vomiting, and tenesmus are also common. Physical examination may reveal diffuse abdominal tenderness, fever, and signs of dehydration, such as dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, and hypotension. Laboratory findings often include leukocytosis with a left shift and the presence of blood or mucus in stool samples. Blood and stool cultures are essential for confirming the diagnosis and determining antibiotic susceptibility, although cultures may be negative in some cases. Additional tests, such as enzyme-linked immunoassay (ELISA), polymerase chain reaction (PCR), or colon biopsies, may be necessary for hospitalized or high-risk patients. Treatment involves oral rehydration with solutions containing water, glucose, and electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, chloride, and bicarbonate. Intravenous fluids are reserved for patients with severe dehydration or those unable to tolerate oral intake. Antibiotic therapy is recommended for all patients and typically includes a 3-day course of ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, or extended-spectrum penicillins.
